solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Returning show restricted by extremely corny humour (6)

indicators.note: coming back, so the word runs the other way
the outside letters hem the show in
at the extremes: just the first and last letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of CornY
DEMO (a show, a demonstration) turned round

annotation.surface: A tired old comedy show comes back on air, still weighed down by its corny jokes.
annotation.walkthrough: OMED sits between C and Y, the two ends of 'corny'. The whole surface is about comedy, so the definition hides in plain sight at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: Comedy is humour, the funny stuff itself.

entries.clue: Guy friends draw parallels between adopting daughter and son (9)

indicators.note: taking something in, as a family takes in a child

blocks.note: to compare two things is to draw parallels between them
d = daughter, taken inside COMPARE
s = son, added at the end

annotation.surface: Someone compares two male friends who have adopted a daughter as well as having a son.
annotation.walkthrough: COMPARE takes in D to give COMPADRE, and S makes it plural. 'Between' belongs to the verb phrase, not to the placing of the D.
annotation.definitionFit: Compadres are pals or mates, borrowed from Spanish; 'guy friends' is a loose, playful way of putting it.

entries.clue: Virile guards fighting Trojan? (7)

indicators.note: the outer word stands around the inner one, as a guard surrounds what it protects

blocks.note: virile = male, manly
fighting = war, placed inside MALE

annotation.surface: A manly warrior stands guard in the Trojan War.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the Trojan is not from Troy but a Trojan horse, a program that sneaks harmful code onto a computer.
annotation.definitionFit: A Trojan is one kind of malicious software, so it is an example of malware.

entries.clue: Departs too soon, at significant cost (6)

blocks.note: d = departs, as on a train timetable
too soon = early

annotation.surface: Someone leaves before they should, and it costs them a great deal.
annotation.walkthrough: D for 'departs' is the timetable abbreviation. The surface suggests an untimely death, which chimes with 'dearly departed'.
annotation.definitionFit: To pay dearly is to pay at great cost.

entries.clue: Name a soft drink containing a hint of orange (7)

indicators.note: the drink holds the next piece inside it
just a trace: the first letter

blocks.note: taken as it stands
p = piano, soft in music
a pint, the usual drink
the first letter of Orange, placed inside PINT

annotation.surface: Someone asks for a soft drink with a dash of orange in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soft drink' reads as one thing, but 'soft' is P and 'drink' is PINT. Also 'Name' looks like a noun at the front, and it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to name someone for a role is to choose them for it.

entries.clue: Racehorse runs into lake, uncontrollably (5)

indicators.note: puts the R in among the other letters
out of control, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: r = runs, from cricket scoring
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A bolting racehorse charges into a lake, out of control.
annotation.walkthrough: Arkle was a famous Irish steeplechaser of the 1960s, winner of three Cheltenham Gold Cups.
annotation.definitionFit: Arkle is perhaps the best-known racehorse in jump racing history.

entries.clue: Ready to keep on getting corrupted (8)

indicators.note: one word holds on to another inside it

blocks.note: poised = ready to act
taken as it stands, inside POISED

annotation.surface: Someone stands ready to keep going as things slowly turn bad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ready to keep on' reads as eager to carry on, but 'to keep' is the instruction and 'on' is simply itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Poison is used figuratively for any corrupting influence, as in minds turned against someone.

entries.clue: Time for a quick coffee? (7)

blocks.note: time as a noun: a moment, a split second
the freeze-dried kind, made by stirring granules into hot water

annotation.surface: Is it time for a quick cup of coffee?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time for a coffee?' reads as a break at work. The question mark marks 'quick coffee' as a sly way of describing the freeze-dried kind.
annotation.definitionFit: The noun means a moment, and the adjective describes coffee made from soluble granules in seconds.

entries.clue: Action of lifting the foot (5)

blocks.note: taken as it stands
ft = foot, the unit of length

annotation.surface: A description of raising your foot off the ground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifting the foot' paints someone taking a step, but 'lifting' means stealing, as in shoplifting.
annotation.definitionFit: Lifting is slang for stealing, so the act of lifting is theft.

entries.clue: Writer gets rising pulse (8)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: to net something is to get it
dhal is a lentil or split pea, a pulse

annotation.surface: A writer finds his pulse racing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' suggests a heartbeat but means an edible seed. Stendhal was the French novelist who wrote The Red and the Black.
annotation.definitionFit: Stendhal was a nineteenth-century French writer.

entries.clue: Spice Girl accompanying a legendary soprano (5)

blocks.note: Mel B, Scary Spice of the Spice Girls
taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A pop star sings alongside a famous opera singer.
annotation.walkthrough: The Spice Girls had two Mels, and only Mel B fits. Nellie Melba was the Australian soprano after whom peach Melba and Melba toast are named.
annotation.definitionFit: Dame Nellie Melba was one of the most celebrated sopranos of all time.

entries.clue: Call into question opinion given by magazine? (4,5)

blocks.note: someone's take on a matter is their opinion
an issue of a magazine; the question mark admits an issue is only one copy of it

annotation.surface: Someone doubts a view published in a magazine.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a magazine column, which is where both halves come from: a writer's take and the issue that prints it.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for disputing or disagreeing with something, which is questioning it.

entries.clue: A way of identifying weapon immediately (2,1,6)

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a tag is a label that identifies something
a lance is a knight's spear

annotation.surface: A weapon can be identified straight away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A way of identifying' looks like a single phrase, but the A stands alone and the rest is TAG.
annotation.definitionFit: To see something at a glance is to take it in immediately.

entries.clue: Collection of books covering standard, illusionary works (2,3)

indicators.note: the books wrap around the standard

blocks.note: OT = Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible
par = the standard, as in golf

annotation.surface: A library shelf of books that hides a standard set of illusions.
annotation.walkthrough: OT is the crossword's usual Old Testament. Op art is the 1960s style of optical illusion painting, made famous by Bridget Riley.
annotation.definitionFit: Op art uses patterns that trick the eye, so its works are illusionary.

entries.clue: Instrument does maybe turn around (4)

indicators.note: face the other way, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: does are female deer; 'maybe' marks them as one example

annotation.surface: A musical instrument does maybe spin round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the verb 'do', but it is the plural of doe, a female deer.
annotation.definitionFit: A reed is a wind instrument, or the vibrating strip in one; in the loose sense it names the instrument itself.

entries.clue: Teacher fabricated rubbish about God (3,7)

indicators.note: made up, so the letters are rearranged
turned round, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: TEACHER rearranged
ROT (rubbish) turned round

annotation.surface: A teacher spreads made-up nonsense about God.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like it means 'concerning', which is how the surface reads it, but it reverses ROT.
annotation.definitionFit: God is called the Creator, maker of heaven and earth.

entries.clue: Cheered up after games machine finally arrived (8)

indicators.note: the letter from 'arrived' follows the machine
'finally' means at the end, so only the last letter of the word is taken

blocks.note: a games console, such as a PlayStation
the last letter of arriveD

annotation.surface: Someone felt happier once the new games console finally turned up.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a delivery that brightens someone's day, which is almost the definition itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: comforting someone after a let-down cheers them up.

entries.clue: Dissident about to join family heading north (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards

blocks.note: re = about, concerning
to fuse is to join
kin = family

annotation.surface: A dissident is about to rejoin their family by travelling north.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is RE and 'to join' is FUSE.
annotation.definitionFit: Refuseniks were Soviet Jews refused permission to emigrate; the word now means any protester who refuses to comply.

entries.clue: Love in Macbeth represented great sacrifice (8)

indicators.note: puts the O among the other letters
presented again in another form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: love = nil = O in tennis
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: In a staging of Macbeth, love turns out to be a great sacrifice.
annotation.walkthrough: Fittingly, Hecate is the witch goddess who appears in Macbeth.
annotation.definitionFit: A hecatomb was originally a sacrifice of a hundred oxen in ancient Greece, and so any great sacrifice or slaughter.

entries.clue: Bird of course mostly seen in wild gardens (10)

indicators.note: most of the word, so the last letter goes
something seen in a place is inside it, so these letters go inside the others
untamed, so the letters run free

blocks.note: GARDENS rearranged
LINE (a course, as in a line of action) without its last letter, set inside

annotation.surface: A bird of the kind you would expect to spot in overgrown gardens.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of course' reads as 'naturally' but is a noun phrase: a course is a line. The sanderling is a small wading bird that races along the edge of the surf.
annotation.definitionFit: The sanderling is a small sandpiper, a bird of sandy beaches.

entries.clue: Emissions target number set up. It means nothing! (3,4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised up means reading from the bottom

blocks.note: TEN, a number, turned upside down
zero means nothing, nil

annotation.surface: A cynic dismisses a climate target as a number that means nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation reads as a jibe at climate pledges, which makes the surface feel topical while it spells out ZERO.
annotation.definitionFit: Net zero is the goal of balancing greenhouse gas emissions against removals.

entries.clue: Parsnip oddly lacking flavour at first? Yeah, right! (2,2)

indicators.note: without the odd-numbered letters, leaving the even ones
'at first' means at the beginning, so only the word's opening letter is used

blocks.note: PARSNIP without letters 1, 3, 5, 7 leaves A, S, I
the first letter of Flavour

annotation.surface: Someone scoffs at the claim that a parsnip lacks flavour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'As if!' is a scornful reply meaning much the same as the sarcastic 'Yeah, right!'
annotation.definitionFit: Both are sarcastic retorts of disbelief.

entries.clue: Colourful arrays of Bond baddies very nearly dead just before the end (7)

indicators.note: almost all of the word: the last letter goes
the letter immediately before the last one

blocks.note: SPECTRE, the villainous organisation in the James Bond films, losing its last letter
the letter just before the final D of deAd

annotation.surface: Bond villains are within a whisker of being killed just before the film's finale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very nearly dead' looks like one phrase about the baddies, but 'very nearly' clips SPECTRE and 'dead' is only mined for one letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Spectra are bands of colour, like the rainbow from a prism.

entries.clue: Film, we’re told, wasn’t a hit (6)

indicators.note: what we hear said, so the word goes by its sound

blocks.note: a film of mist, a thin haze

annotation.surface: Reportedly the film flopped at the box office.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Film' and 'hit' both suggest cinema, but the film is a thin layer, like mist on a window.
annotation.definitionFit: A shot or throw that failed to strike its target is the opposite of a hit.

entries.clue: Empty spaces in front of Tate taken on by an esteemed artist (5)

indicators.note: the front of the word: its first letter
taken aboard, so it goes inside

blocks.note: taken as it stands
the first letter of Tate
RA = Royal Academician, an honoured British artist

annotation.surface: An esteemed artist is hired for empty spaces outside the Tate gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tate is a group of London art galleries, which suits the RA. Antra (singular antrum) are cavities, especially in bone.
annotation.definitionFit: An antrum is an anatomical cavity, so antra are empty spaces.

entries.clue: Type of suit that’s partially water-resistant, I guess (4-1)

indicators.note: only part of the words is used

blocks.note: inside resistANT I Guess

annotation.surface: Someone guesses that a certain suit is partly waterproof.
annotation.walkthrough: An anti-G suit is worn by fighter pilots to stop blood draining from the head under high g-forces; the surface points to a wetsuit instead.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by type: the pressurised garment pilots wear against g-forces is one kind of suit.

entries.clue: Bachelor being slimy and being inclined to insobriety (9)

blocks.note: b = bachelor, as in BA
the state of being slimy, turned into a noun to match the definition

annotation.surface: A slimy single man with a fondness for drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Being' appears twice to keep the two halves parallel: each is a noun describing a condition.
annotation.definitionFit: Booziness is a tendency to drink too much, and insobriety is drunkenness.

entries.clue: Aerospace company dismissing old person (5)

indicators.note: sending away, so the letter is removed

blocks.note: the American aircraft maker
o = old, the letter sent away

annotation.surface: An aircraft firm lays off an older employee.
annotation.walkthrough: o = old is a standard abbreviation. The surface reads as a news item about redundancy.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the general sense of a living individual, a human.

entries.clue: Helicopter shortly to be scrambled for law enforcers (3,6)

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter goes
mixed up, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: HELICOPTER without its last letter; anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A police helicopter is about to be scrambled for an emergency.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scrambled' reads as sending aircraft up in a hurry, the natural sense for a helicopter, but here it mixes the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The police are the people who enforce the law.

entries.clue: Demonstrated, perhaps, what couturiers may use (5)

blocks.note: read as two words: took part in a protest by occupying a place
a glossy fabric that fashion houses work in

annotation.surface: Fashion designers were seen at a protest, showing off what they make.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrated' looks like 'showed', but the 'perhaps' points to protest: one way to demonstrate is to sit in.
annotation.definitionFit: Protesters who sat in demonstrated; couturiers are high-fashion designers, who work in satin.

entries.clue: Continue to obtain cheap Aussie wine from here? (4,3)

blocks.note: to go on is to continue
to bag something is to get hold of it

annotation.surface: Someone keeps going back for more cheap Australian wine.
annotation.walkthrough: A goon bag is the foil bladder inside an Australian box of wine; 'goon' is slang for cheap wine. The question mark covers the definition by location.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheap Aussie wine is poured from the goon bag, so that is where it comes from.

entries.clue: Deadhead ultimately invested in excellent selection of albums? (2,4)

indicators.note: at the end: the last letter
put inside, as money is put into something

blocks.note: crack = first-rate, as in crack troops
the last letter of DeadheaD, placed inside CRACK

annotation.surface: A Grateful Dead fan puts money into a fine record collection.
annotation.walkthrough: A Deadhead is a fan of the Grateful Dead, which suits the music surface. The question mark admits a rack is where a selection of albums is kept.
annotation.definitionFit: A CD rack holds a collection of albums on compact disc.
